documents.title: Journey 1: Foundations: from a question to data
documents.summary: Statistics starts before the first calculation: define the population, the sample, the variable type and the branch of analysis. This journey builds the vocabulary the other eight journeys depend on.
keywords: What are we measuring, who is it about, and what can a number even claim?
Distinguish a population from a sample, and a parameter from a statistic.
Classify an observation as numerical or categorical, and explain what that permits.
Say whether a question is descriptive or inferential before choosing a method.

documents.title: Journey 2: Describe the data you actually have
documents.summary: Mean, median and mode answer different questions; variance, standard deviation and IQR measure different units. The visual layer lets you move one point and watch resistance and sensitivity diverge.
keywords: Where is the centre, how wide is the spread, and which summary survives an outlier?
Read mean, median and mode as different summaries, not interchangeable ones.
Explain why the mean moves more than the median when an outlier is added.
Use the n−1 denominator for a sample and say what the IQR's middle 50% means.

documents.title: Journey 3: Probability: the space of what could happen
documents.summary: Probability is a measure over a sample space, not a feeling about a sentence. The lab makes complements, intersections, conditional probability, independence and mutual exclusivity visible in the same space.
keywords: Where does probability live, and how do events combine?
Compute a complement, an intersection and a conditional probability from the same event.
Explain why mutually exclusive events are not independent.
Distinguish a discrete probability mass from a continuous density.

documents.title: Journey 4: Distributions: shapes with rules
documents.summary: Binomial counts successes in fixed independent trials; Poisson counts events in a fixed interval; the normal describes a continuous symmetric bell. Each has a different support, parameter meaning and probability rule.
keywords: Which distribution matches the data-generating process, and what are its assumptions?
Check the four binomial conditions before using a binomial model.
Read a normal probability as area and a z-score as distance in standard deviations.
Explain why λ is a rate per stated interval, not a probability.

documents.title: Journey 5: Sampling and estimation: from one sample to a range
documents.summary: The central limit theorem is about the distribution of sample means, not about individual observations becoming normal. Standard error and confidence intervals turn that sampling distribution into a calibrated statement.
keywords: How variable is a statistic, and how do we express uncertainty without pretending it is certainty?
Keep the population, one sample and the sampling distribution visually distinct.
Compute and interpret SE = σ/√n and explain why n quadrupling halves it.
Interpret a 95% interval as a property of the procedure, not a probability about a fixed parameter.

documents.title: Journey 6: Hypothesis testing: evidence under a null model
documents.summary: A test compares an observed statistic with the distribution it would have under H₀. The p-value is a tail area conditional on that model; α is chosen before the data; failing to reject is not accepting.
keywords: If the null were true, how unusual is what we observed — and what decision follows?
Write H₀ and Hₐ and choose a sidedness before looking at the result.
Read a p-value as P(statistic at least as extreme | H₀), never P(H₀ true).
Distinguish Type I from Type II error and statistical from practical significance.

documents.title: Journey 7: Experimental design: earning a causal claim
documents.summary: Randomization, control, blinding and a pre-specified outcome are the design features that make groups comparable. The A/B test is one randomized design, not the definition of all experiments.
keywords: What has to be true about the design before a difference can support a causal sentence?
Identify treatment, control, response and the unit of assignment.
Explain what randomization balances in expectation — and what it does not guarantee.
Distinguish single-blind, double-blind and open-label designs without overclaiming.

documents.title: Journey 8: Relationships and causality: what r can and cannot say
documents.summary: Pearson r measures the strength and direction of a linear association. It is not a slope, it can be near zero under a strong curve, and observational co-movement is not a causal effect.
keywords: Is the association linear, could a third variable explain it, and what would a causal claim require?
Read a scatterplot before trusting a correlation coefficient.
Explain why r ≈ 0 does not rule out a strong non-linear relationship.
Separate correlation, regression slope and a causal effect in plain language.

documents.title: Journey 9: Synthesis: choose, check, decide, explain
documents.summary: The final journey turns the reference into a decision aid: a connected mental model, a formula workbench, a tool navigator, misconception cards, the checkout case and a printable field guide.
keywords: Given a new question, which tool applies — and what would make the answer irresponsible?
Route a new question to a defensible method and name its assumptions.
Use the formula sheet without detaching a formula from its conditions.
Tell the checkout story end to end with consistent denominators and honest uncertainty.

documents.title: 1. The big picture: what is statistics
documents.summary: “A statistic is the same thing as a parameter.” A statistic is computed from a sample and varies; a parameter describes the population and is usually unknown.
keywords: Name the six stages from data to decision and say what each one produces.
Use population, sample, parameter and statistic correctly in one sentence.

documents.title: 2. Data types and what they permit
documents.summary: “If it is written with digits, it is numerical.” Customer IDs and phone numbers are labels; averaging them is meaningless.
keywords: Sort observations into numerical (discrete/continuous) and categorical (nominal/ordinal).
Explain why a numeric-looking identifier is categorical and why ordinal ranks are not measurements.

documents.title: 3. Descriptive vs inferential statistics
documents.summary: “A sample summary is already a conclusion about the population.” Description stops at the data; inference adds a model, uncertainty and assumptions.
keywords: Tell a statement about the observed sample from a claim about the wider population.
Identify which branch a question belongs to before computing anything.

documents.title: 4. Measures of center
documents.summary: “The mean is always the best centre.” In a skewed distribution or with outliers, the mean is pulled toward the tail and may stop representing a typical value.
keywords: Compute mean, median and mode and explain when each is the better summary.
Predict which of mean and median moves further when one extreme value is added.

documents.title: 5. Measures of spread
documents.summary: “Standard deviation and standard error are interchangeable.” SD describes individual values; SE describes how a statistic varies across repeated samples.
keywords: Distinguish range, variance, standard deviation and IQR by what they measure and their units.
Explain the n−1 sample denominator and the 1.5×IQR outlier rule.

documents.title: 6. Probability, complements, independence and conditionals
documents.summary: “Independent means the events cannot happen together.” Independence is about information: knowing B does not change P(A). Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together at all.
keywords: Compute P(Aᶜ), P(A∩B), P(A∪B) and P(A|B) from a sample space.
Explain why two mutually exclusive events with positive probability cannot be independent.

documents.title: 7. Probability distributions: mass vs density
documents.summary: “The height of the normal curve is the probability of that value.” Height is density; probability is area under the curve between two values.
keywords: Read a PMF bar as a probability and a PDF area as a probability.
State why the probability of one exact value under a continuous distribution is zero.

documents.title: 8. The binomial distribution
documents.summary: “Binomial counts how many trials happen.” It counts successes among a fixed number of trials; the number of trials is an input, not the outcome.
keywords: Check the fixed-n, independent-trial, constant-p, binary-outcome conditions.
Compute P(X=k), a lower tail or an upper tail and read E(X)=np and Var(X)=np(1−p).

documents.title: 9. The normal distribution and z-scores
documents.summary: “Changing σ changes the total probability.” The total area stays 1; a larger σ flattens and widens the curve.
keywords: Locate a value on a normal curve and shade the corresponding area.
Standardize with z=(x−μ)/σ and apply the 68–95–99.7 rule as an approximation.

documents.title: 10. The Poisson distribution
documents.summary: “λ=20 means P(X=20) is high, so 20 is the mode.” λ is a mean count; at integer λ the mode is actually the pair λ−1 and λ.
keywords: Define λ as the mean count per fixed interval and compute exact and tail probabilities.
Verify E(X)=Var(X)=λ and explain the discrete support.

documents.title: 11. The central limit theorem
documents.summary: “The CLT says the data become normal once n is large.” It is the sampling distribution of the mean that approaches normality, not the population or a single sample.
keywords: Explain that the distribution of sample means tends toward normality under stated conditions.
Show that the mean of the sampling distribution equals μ.

documents.title: 12. Sampling distribution
documents.summary: “A sampling distribution is just a bigger sample.” It is the distribution of a statistic over repeated samples — a different object with a different axis.
keywords: Distinguish the population distribution, one sample's distribution and the sampling distribution.
Label each panel with its own unit and axis.

documents.title: 13. Standard error
documents.summary: “SE is the SD of the data divided by √n because the data got narrower.” The data distribution did not change; the sampling distribution of the mean did.
keywords: Compute SE = σ/√n and its estimated form s/√n.
Explain why SE shrinks as n grows while the SD of the values stays put.

documents.title: 14. Confidence intervals
documents.summary: “There is a 95% probability that the fixed parameter is inside this interval.” Once computed, the interval either covers the fixed parameter or does not; 95% is the long-run coverage of the method.
keywords: Build estimate ± critical value × SE and explain each term.
Interpret 95% coverage as a property of repeated procedures.

documents.title: 15. Hypothesis testing and the two hypotheses
documents.summary: “The test calculates the probability that H₀ is true.” It calculates the probability of data at least this extreme assuming H₀ is true.
keywords: Write a null and an alternative for a comparison, including sidedness.
Explain why the null is a model to test, not a belief to prove.

documents.title: 16. The hypothesis-testing workflow
documents.summary: “The workflow starts with a p-value.” It starts with the question, the populations and the hypotheses; the statistic comes later.
keywords: Order the seven stages from populations to a qualified conclusion.
Identify the decision point where α enters.

documents.title: 17. Sampling variability inside a test
documents.summary: “A difference between sample means proves a difference between populations.” Samples vary; the test asks whether the observed difference is unusual under H₀.
keywords: Show that two samples can differ even when the population means are equal.
Reframe the question as whether the difference is larger than sampling noise.

documents.title: 18. Test statistic and standard error
documents.summary: “A test statistic of 3.6 is a 3.6% probability.” It is a distance in SE units; the probability comes from the null distribution, not from the number itself.
keywords: Express a test statistic as a distance measured in standard errors.
Reproduce (5.4 − 0)/1.5 = 3.6 and explain what the 3.6 means.

documents.title: 19. The p-value
documents.summary: “The p-value is the overlap between the null and alternative curves.” It is a tail area of the null sampling distribution, not an overlap.
keywords: Define a p-value conditional on H₀ and the chosen sidedness.
Distinguish the p-value area from an overlap between two distributions.

documents.title: 20. The significance level α
documents.summary: “α is the probability that the result is wrong.” α is the long-run false-positive rate under H₀ for the chosen rule.
keywords: Explain α as a pre-declared Type I error rate and decision threshold.
Show why moving α after seeing p changes the rule, not the evidence.

documents.title: 21. The decision rule
documents.summary: “Failing to reject proves H₀.” Absence of sufficient evidence against H₀ is not evidence that H₀ is exactly true.
keywords: Apply p ≤ α → reject H₀ and p > α → fail to reject H₀.
Avoid the phrase “accept H₀” and explain the boundary case p = α.

documents.title: 22. Type I and Type II errors
documents.summary: “Type I and Type II errors are complements.” They are conditional on different states of reality; α + β is not 1 in general.
keywords: Map the four reality × decision cells and name the two errors.
Relate α to Type I error and β to Type II error under a specified alternative.

documents.title: 23. Statistical vs practical significance
documents.summary: “Statistically significant means important.” Significance is about compatibility with H₀; importance depends on effect size, context and cost.
keywords: Separate evidence against H₀ from the size and business value of an effect.
Explain how a huge sample can make a trivial difference significant.

documents.title: 24. Experiments
documents.summary: “Any comparison is an experiment.” Without manipulation and a design that controls alternatives, it is an observational comparison.
keywords: Identify the treatment and the response in a causal question.
Explain what manipulating the treatment buys over observing it.

documents.title: 25. Controlled experiments
documents.summary: “Control means do nothing.” A control can receive a placebo or the current standard, and the point is a comparable reference.
keywords: Describe the role of a treatment group and a control group.
Explain why imbalance on a covariate can create a misleading difference.

documents.title: 26. Randomization
documents.summary: “Randomization guarantees the groups are balanced.” It balances in expectation; any one run can still be imbalanced.
keywords: Explaining randomization as a design device, not a data-cleaning step.
Show balance in expectation and finite-sample imbalance in a seeded shuffle.

documents.title: 27. Blinding and placebo
documents.summary: “Double-blind means the analyst also does not know the hypothesis.” It means participants and the people administering or assessing treatment do not know assignment.
keywords: Distinguish participant blinding, experimenter blinding and double blinding.
Explain what a placebo controls and what blinding cannot fix.

documents.title: 28. RCT vs A/B testing
documents.summary: “A/B testing and RCTs are unrelated.” An A/B test is a randomized controlled experiment applied to a product change.
keywords: Explain that an A/B test is a two-arm randomized design, not the definition of an RCT.

documents.title: 29. Independent and dependent variables
documents.summary: “Whatever is on the X axis causes the Y.” Axis placement is a convention; only the design supports a causal reading.
keywords: Map the predictor/treatment to X and the response to Y in a scenario.
Explain why the role is defined by the question, not by the axis label.

documents.title: 30. Correlation and Pearson r
documents.summary: “r is the slope.” r is standardized covariance; the slope depends on the units of X and Y and is not bounded by 1.
keywords: Read direction and linear strength from r and from the scatterplot.
Explain why r is unitless and bounded in [−1, 1].

documents.title: 31. Pearson correlation and linear relationships
documents.summary: “r ≈ 0 means no relationship.” It means no *linear* relationship; a U-shape or cycle can be strongly dependent.
keywords: Show that a strong curved pattern can produce r near zero.
Restrict Pearson interpretation to linear association.

documents.title: 32. Correlation is not causation
documents.summary: “A high r proves X causes Y.” Association is compatible with reverse causation, confounding and coincidence.
keywords: Separate co-movement from a causal effect.
Name the alternative explanations that an observational r cannot exclude.

documents.title: 33. Confounding variables
documents.summary: “If the correlation is strong, a confounder cannot explain it.” A strong pooled association can be entirely produced or reversed by a third variable.
keywords: Draw a third-variable structure Z→X, Z→Y and explain the induced association.
Show what happens to a pooled correlation after within-group separation.

documents.title: 34. Correlation vs experiment
documents.summary: “A correlation study can establish causality if the sample is big enough.” Sample size narrows uncertainty; it does not remove confounding.
keywords: Choose the tool based on the question's evidential target.
Explain why a randomized experiment supports a stronger causal claim than an association.

documents.title: 35. Correlation vs regression
documents.summary: “r=0.8 means Y rises 0.8 units per unit of X.” That is a slope statement; r has no units.
keywords: Read a regression slope with units and compare it with r.
Show that positive affine rescaling changes the slope but not r.

documents.title: 36. How the topics connect
documents.summary: “The topics are independent chapters.” Each later method depends on the sampling and probability ideas built earlier.
keywords: Trace the prerequisite path from description to decision.
Locate a concept in the atlas and open its source section.

documents.title: 37. The formula index
documents.summary: “The formula is the method.” A formula without its assumptions and data requirements is not a valid analysis.
keywords: Match each formula to the question it answers and the conditions it requires.
Read every symbol and unit without detaching it from its section.

documents.title: 38. Decision rules: when the question changes
documents.summary: “The most advanced method is the safest.” The right method is the one whose assumptions the data and design can support.
keywords: Route a new question to a starting method and name its alternatives.
See which inputs and assumptions the method requires before it is used.

documents.title: 39. The mistakes to avoid
documents.summary: “Memorising the wrong sentence is enough to avoid it.” Each myth needs a concrete counterexample and a corrected sentence.
keywords: Recognise the ten misconceptions and the counterexample that defeats each.
Use the correction without hiding the original claim.

documents.title: 40. The end-to-end checkout case
documents.summary: “A significant lift is automatically worth shipping.” The decision also needs effect size, cost, risk and a pre-specified meaningful threshold.
keywords: Carry one scenario from question through assignment, data, test, decision and business interpretation.
Keep denominators and uncertainty consistent across every panel.

documents.title: 41. Final mental model
documents.summary: “A decision is just the p-value.” The decision combines evidence, uncertainty, effect size, cost and context.
keywords: Describe the layered system from population to decision in one pass.
Say where uncertainty, confounding and assumptions enter.

documents.title: 42. One-page cheat sheet
documents.summary: “A cheat sheet is a substitute for the lesson.” It is an index back to the lesson and its qualifications.
keywords: Use a compact, printable field guide without losing the conditions.
Scan the formula, the question and the caution together.

documents.title: 43. Course conclusion
documents.summary: “The final answer is a number.” The final answer is a qualified decision with an explicit limitation.
keywords: Run the transferable process: question → design → data → method → evidence → decision.
Name the limitation that would change the conclusion.

Reject the null when p is less than or equal to alpha; fail to reject it when p is greater than alpha.

documents.title: Population
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The complete set of units a question is about. Its summary is a parameter.

documents.title: Sample
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A subset of the population that is actually observed. Its summary is a statistic.

documents.title: Parameter
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A fixed, usually unknown population quantity such as μ or σ.

documents.title: Statistic
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A quantity computed from sample data, such as x̄ or s; it varies from sample to sample.

documents.title: Descriptive statistics
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Summaries of the observed data, with no claim beyond those observations.

documents.title: Inferential statistics
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Generalising from a sample to a population using a model and quantified uncertainty.

documents.title: Mean
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The sum of values divided by n. Sensitive to outliers.

documents.title: Median
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The middle value after sorting; resistant to outliers.

documents.title: Mode
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The most frequent value; there may be several modes or none.

documents.title: Standard deviation
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The square root of variance, in the original units; spread of individual values.

documents.title: IQR
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Q₃ − Q₁, the range of the middle 50% of the data; resistant to outliers.

documents.title: Outlier
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A value unusually far from the bulk of the data; in a box plot, beyond 1.5×IQR fences.

documents.title: Complement
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The event that A does not occur: P(Aᶜ)=1−P(A).

documents.title: Conditional probability
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: P(A|B), the probability of A after restricting the sample space to B.

documents.title: Independence
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Knowing one event occurred does not change the probability of the other: P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B).

documents.title: Mutually exclusive
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Events that cannot occur together, so P(A∩B)=0. Not the same as independent.

documents.title: PMF
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A discrete probability mass function: each value has a probability, and the masses sum to 1.

documents.title: PDF
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A continuous density: probability is area under the curve, and a single point has probability zero.

documents.title: Binomial distribution
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The count of successes in n independent trials with constant success probability p.

documents.title: Normal distribution
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A symmetric continuous bell curve defined by μ and σ, with total area 1.

documents.title: Z-score
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: z=(x−μ)/σ, the signed number of standard deviations from the mean.

documents.title: Empirical rule
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: For a roughly normal distribution, about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of values lie within 1, 2 and 3 SD of the mean.

documents.title: Poisson distribution
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A count distribution for events in a fixed interval with mean λ; mean equals variance.

documents.title: Lambda (λ)
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The Poisson mean count per stated interval — a rate, not a probability.

documents.title: Central limit theorem
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Under suitable conditions, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as n grows.

documents.title: Sampling distribution
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The distribution of a statistic over repeated samples of the same size from the same population.

documents.title: Standard error
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The standard deviation of a statistic's sampling distribution; for the mean, σ/√n.

documents.title: Confidence interval
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: An interval produced by a procedure with a stated long-run coverage rate.

documents.title: Coverage
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The long-run proportion of intervals from a procedure that contain the fixed parameter.

documents.title: Null hypothesis
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The model of no difference or no effect used to derive the null sampling distribution.

documents.title: Alternative hypothesis
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The claim being assessed; its direction determines what counts as more extreme.

documents.title: Test statistic
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A standardized distance between the observed result and the value expected under H₀.

documents.title: p-value
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: P(statistic at least as extreme as observed | H₀ true). Not P(H₀ true).

documents.title: Alpha (α)
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The pre-declared Type I error threshold; reject H₀ when p≤α.

documents.title: Type I error
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Rejecting a true H₀ — a false positive, with rate α under the null.

documents.title: Type II error
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Failing to reject a false H₀ — a false negative, with rate β under a specified alternative.

documents.title: Power
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: 1−β: the probability of rejecting H₀ when a specified alternative is true.

documents.title: Practical significance
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Whether an effect is large enough to matter in context, independent of statistical detectability.

documents.title: Randomization
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Assigning units to conditions by a random mechanism so groups balance in expectation.

documents.title: Blinding
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: Withholding treatment assignment from participants and/or assessors to reduce expectation effects.

documents.title: RCT
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A controlled experiment that assigns units randomly to treatment conditions.

documents.title: A/B test
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A two-arm randomized experiment comparing a control (A) with a treatment (B).

documents.title: Confounder
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A third variable that affects both X and Y and can create or distort an observed association.

documents.title: Pearson r
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: A unitless measure of the direction and strength of linear association, in [−1,1].

documents.title: Regression slope
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: The expected change in Y per one-unit increase in X, in the units of the data.

documents.title: Absolute lift
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: p_B−p_A in percentage points; the raw difference between two rates.

documents.title: Relative lift
documents.summary: Glossary
keywords: (p_B−p_A)/p_A; the difference as a proportion of the baseline rate.

documents.title: The mean is always the best measure of centre.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Use the median when the distribution is skewed or outliers matter to the question.
In [2,4,4,4,5,5,7,100] the mean jumps above 16 while the median stays at 4.5. One value changes the typical picture.

documents.title: Standard deviation and standard error are the same thing.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: SD = spread of observations; SE = spread of a statistic across repeated samples.
The SD describes individual values and stays roughly fixed as n grows; SE=σ/√n shrinks because it describes the sample mean.

documents.title: A p-value is the probability that H₀ is true.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Read it as a compatibility check with the null model, never as the posterior probability of the null.
The p-value is computed *assuming* H₀. It is P(data at least this extreme | H₀), not P(H₀ | data).

documents.title: The p-value is the overlap between the null and alternative distributions.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Shade the equally-or-more-extreme region under H₀; do not shade the alternative.
Overlap involves both distributions; the p-value uses only the null sampling distribution and the observed statistic's tail.

documents.title: If p > α, we accept H₀.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Say “fail to reject H₀” and describe the uncertainty and the alternative explanations.
A non-significant result means the data are compatible with H₀ at this threshold; it does not establish that H₀ is exactly true.

documents.title: You can choose α after seeing the p-value.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Declare α, the test and the sidedness before looking at the data.
Choosing the threshold after the result changes the rule and inflates the false-positive rate. α is part of the design, fixed before analysis.

documents.title: Statistically significant means practically important.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Report the effect size and its interval against a pre-specified meaningful threshold.
With a large enough n, a 0.01-percentage-point difference can produce p<0.05 while being commercially irrelevant.

documents.title: r ≈ 0 means X and Y are unrelated.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Look at the scatterplot; r measures linear association only.
A symmetric U-shape has strong dependence but r near 0, because positive and negative linear contributions cancel.

documents.title: A strong correlation proves causation.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Causal claims need design — random assignment, control, or another credible identification strategy.
Ice-cream sales and drowning correlate because both follow temperature. A third variable can create the association without either causing the other.

documents.title: r=0.8 means Y increases by 0.8 units when X increases by one unit.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Report the slope with units separately from r.
r is unitless and bounded by ±1; the slope is r·sᵧ/sₓ and changes when the units of X or Y change.

documents.title: Randomization makes the two groups identical.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Check baseline balance and pre-specify adjustments; report the assignment mechanism.
Randomization balances covariates in expectation. A particular shuffle can still put more older participants in one arm.

documents.title: There is a 95% probability that this computed interval contains μ.
documents.summary: Misconceptions
keywords: Say “95% of intervals built this way would cover μ” and state the assumptions.
μ is fixed. The procedure covers μ in about 95% of repeated samples; this particular interval either covers it or does not.
